transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-28
Time: 10:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Price (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (NimbleHealth ML), Miguel Torres (NimbleHealth Platform), Leah Chen (NimbleHealth CTO)

Summary:
Quick throughput-focused sync on the POC. Reviewed last week's benchmark results, discussed continuous batching and concurrency tuning, talked about queue/backpressure behavior at high QPS, and agreed next steps for a larger Dedicated canary and more realistic traffic shaping. Action items noted.

Topics:
- Benchmark results review (end-to-end latency vs token throughput)
- Continuous batching configuration and tradeoffs
- Concurrency targets and autoscaling behavior
- Queueing/backpressure + degraded-mode fallbacks
- Next steps: benchmarks, configs, pricing, canary schedule

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Alright, hey everyone thanks for jumping on. This is our weekly POC sync, throughput track. We have about 45 minutes, we wanted to review the numbers Samir ran last week and then agree next steps. Aisha, Miguel, Leah, you good?
[00:12] Aisha: Yep, all good. Thanks.
[00:15] Miguel: Good morning.
[00:16] Leah: Morning.
[00:22] Samir: Quick note before we start, some of the logs we pulled had timestamps a bit off — fireflies transcript might show a couple mis-words. I'll walk through raw CSV and the chart links after.
[00:30] Jordan: Perfect. Samir do you want to kick off with the benchmark summary?
[00:34] Samir: Yeah. So the end-to-end test we ran last Thursday: synthetic workload, uniform request size of ~350 tokens average, we ran with three settings: baseline (no explicit batching), continuous batching enabled at 4x and 8x, and concurrency targets of 4, 8, and 16. We also toggled the KV cache warm vs cold.
[01:05] Samir: High level: continuous batching improved token throughput per GPU by about 2.2x at 8x batch with minimal p95 latency regression when concurrency was moderate. But when we pushed concurrency to 16 the queueing delay grew and tail latency hit the SLO edge.
[01:20] Aisha: Can you clarify queueing delay — is that client side or inside the Redwood runtime queue?
[01:25] Samir: It's inside the runtime's request queue. Basically requests wait a small window to be batched. At higher concurrency, the batch build-up plus exec time caused a longer waiting time in the batch queue. So p50 latency looked fine, but p95 and p99 rose.
[01:38] Miguel: Do we have numbers — like p95 numbers? What are we seeing relative to our target of 300ms p95 for generation?
[01:45] Samir: With 8x batching + concurrency 8, p95 for end-to-end generation (including network) was ~320-350ms on the hosted test instance we used. With concurrency 16 it jumped to ~560ms. The baseline no-batching at concurrency 4 was about 410ms p95 and cost per token was higher.
[02:05] Leah: So batching helps cost but could hurt latency if we overconcur. We're targeting 300ms p95 in prod so 8x/8 is close but slightly over. Thoughts?
[02:18] Jordan: We should square that with Aisha's real request size distribution — the synthetic uniform tokens may be pessimistic/optimistic depending. Aisha, can you share your percentiles?
[02:28] Aisha: Yeah I can. 50th is 290 tokens, 75th is 420, 95th is 980, tail at 99 around 1.6k tokens. We never actually hit 1.6k often but the p95 matters.
[02:40] Samir: OK that explains the delta. Our synthetic 350 token baseline is around your median, but heavier tails will increase exec time and worsen batch waiting time because long requests hold the GPU longer.
[02:52] Miguel: Any quick wins? Batching window tuning?
[02:55] Samir: Yeah, there are a couple levers: 1) Max batch size + dynamic window — prefer smaller max batch with adaptive short window at high tail. 2) Priority queuing for heavy requests or spike shaping so smaller requests don't get stuck behind a 1.6k token inference. 3) Concurrency caps per host and autoscale thresholds. Also prefix/KV cache warm creates benefits; cold-cache runs are worse.
[03:20] Aisha: About priority queueing — can we do per-route profiles so our high-importance low-latency route is prioritized?
[03:27] Samir: Yes, Redwood supports per-route QoS. We can set a low-latency route with stricter batching windows, lower max batch, and lower concurrency cap. For background or high-throughput routes you choose larger batch and higher concurrency.
[03:38] Leah: How about Dedicated — does Dedicated change the numbers, like less noisy neighbors?
[03:42] Jordan: Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools and you control concurrency per pool. The raw per-GPU throughput is similar but you avoid cross-tenant variance. Also autoscale behavior can be tuned to your SLA. We can share Dedicated pricing implications — it tends to lower cost at scale but has committed pricing.
[03:58] Miguel: We also want to test canary with our traffic shape. What's the recommended approach?
[04:03] Samir: Start with a small Dedicated pool, mirror production traffic for a subset of requests (mirror or shadow), run the same batch/concurrency config, measure p50/p95/p99, and then open a small percentage (1-5%) of real traffic for an A/B. We'll need your traffic trace or replay for realistic results.
[04:19] Aisha: We can provide a 24h request trace with obfuscated content. Will that be sufficient?
[04:23] Samir: Yes, a 24h trace with timestamps and token counts is ideal. Please include header that shows route mapping so we can map per-route QoS.
[04:31] Aisha: Will do — sending by Friday.
[04:33] Jordan: Great. On the batching algorithm: there's also an adaptive batching option that adjusts window based on observed latency so it tries to hit target latency automatically — but it's more complex to tune. We suggest starting with fixed batch sizes and conservative windows then try adaptive once baseline is good.
[04:52] Miguel: Any implications for memory / kv cache when using large batches? We saw OOM once in the cold run.
[04:58] Samir: Large batches increase peak memory. If you combine long sequence lengths (like 1.6k) with large B, you can exceed GPU memory depending on quantization and model size. Options: 1) use quantized model variants (we recommended q4 or q5 for your model family), 2) reduce max batch cap when sequences are long, 3) enable KV cache eviction policies or prefix caching to avoid re-computation.
[05:20] Leah: Is the quantized variant going to affect quality? We are sensitive to hallucinations in clinical content.
[05:27] Samir: Minimal for q4/q5 for this family based on our evals, but we should run your eval prompts. We'll add a quality regression check to the bench.
[05:35] Aisha: Good. Also, what's Redwood's backpressure behavior if queues grow? Does it drop, reject, or throttle?
[05:42] Samir: There's configurable behavior: reject with 429, queue with bounded capacity, tail-drop, or degrade to a smaller model variant automatically. We usually recommend bounded queue + graceful fallback to smaller variant once latency or queue size crosses threshold.
[05:55] Jordan: Many customers prefer graceful degradation over hard rejects for UX reasons. But that depends on business semantics.
[06:02] Miguel: For our use case, failing safe (returning a short summary) is acceptable for some routes; others must be strict. So per-route policy is required.
[06:10] Samir: That's supported. We'll draft a suggested per-route config for your three main routes.
[06:16] Jordan: Let's talk timeline and next benchmarks: Samir, can you run the 8x/16 concurrency synthetic but with a replay of Aisha's 24h trace and share the results? Also include adaptive batching vs fixed.
[06:28] Samir: Yep I will. Expect CSVs and charts. I'll also note memory high-water events. Target to deliver by next Monday 2026-08-02.
[06:35] Aisha: We'll send the trace by Friday 2026-07-30.
[06:38] Leah: On pricing — Jordan you'll send Dedicated vs Hosted cost estimates at the projected sustained QPS?
[06:45] Jordan: Yes I'll circulate a delta worksheet that shows per-token cost at your expected QPS and at Dedicated committed tiers.
[06:51] Miguel: And security asks — we need SOC2 docs and audit log format. Will you attach those?
[06:56] Jordan: I'll attach SOC 2 summary and sample audit log schema after this call. Also include SAML/SSO setup guide.
[07:05] Aisha: One more question — autoscaling react time; we saw spikes in the morning that cause brief latency blips. Can autoscale be tuned to be more conservative?
[07:14] Samir: Yes, autoscale window and thresholds are configurable. For low-latency routes prefer pre-warming capacity rather than aggressive reactive scaling. We can suggest baseline buffer capacity so you don't hit cold starts.
[07:25] Miguel: Are there limits on how many concurrent inferences per host? We saw ECU numbers earlier but not sure the mapping.
[07:31] Samir: You define concurrency per worker; the runtime will enforce max inflight tasks. That number depends on model and GPU memory. Typical range for your model family is 8-16 per GPU when using q4 quantization, lower if full FP16.
[07:45] Jordan: Cool. To recap: Aisha sends traffic trace by Friday, Samir runs replayed benchmarks and shares CSV/charts by 2026-08-02, Jordan shares Dedicated pricing and SOC2 + audit schema by 2026-07-30, and we'll plan a small Dedicated canary week of 2026-08-09.
[08:05] Leah: That works. Any blockers?
[08:08] Aisha: None on our side.
[08:10] Miguel: No.
[08:11] Samir: Noted. I'll also include a recommended per-route QoS config and a quick readme on batch window tuning.
[08:19] Jordan: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up in thread with the docs and links.
[08:24] Leah: Thanks.
[08:25] Meeting end.
